title: Cloudflare K2 Builds Event Streams on R2 Object Storage, at a Second of Produce Latency
gist: Cloudflare launched K2 in public beta, a serverless event streaming service built as a partitioned log on R2 object storage, trading ~1s p99 produce latency for cost and elasticity; Hacker News reaction endorsed object storage as the new data substrate but flagged slower end-to-end tails, steep fan-out consume pricing, and sub-100ms competitors like s2.dev.

themes.theme: Object storage as the new data substrate

insights.claim: Cloudflare's K2 is a serverless event streaming service whose partitioned durable log lives in R2 object storage, explicitly trading latency (about 1s p99 produce) for cost and elasticity.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Another entrant in the object-storage-backed streaming wave pressuring Kafka economics.
insights.quote: The trade-off is latency for cost and elasticity, and Cloudflare names the number: about one second of produce latency at p99.

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter argued object store is quickly becoming the new core data substrate, e.g., 'kafka, but on s3' and 'github, but on s3'.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Structural shift benefits object-storage providers and threatens disk-based data system vendors.
insights.quote: Object store is quickly becoming the new core data substrate.
insights.locator: Commenter psanford set out the broader shift

insights.claim: K2's tech lead agreed that every data system not requiring sub-100ms latency is moving to object storage.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Large swaths of streaming/database workloads may migrate to object storage architectures.

insights.claim: Cloudflare built K2 on R2 because Kafka's assumptions don't fit Pipelines running on ephemeral machine slices across 335+ cities over the public internet; R2 provides eleven nines durability and strongly consistent APIs.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Edge architectures require different streaming primitives than datacenter Kafka.

insights.claim: K2 works around object stores' inability to append by buffering writes in memory and writing batches as segment files, using R2 atomic operations for ordering and offsets with no coordination service; that pause is the latency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Explains the inherent latency floor of pure object-storage streaming designs.

insights.claim: A beta user reported K2 writes under one second but end-to-end delivery latency of p95 2.5s and p99 7.5s; the team said tail latency was higher than expected and Consume API performance needs work.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Product maturity gap versus marketing figures; watch for promised read-latency fixes.
insights.locator: The sharpest exchange came from someone

insights.claim: s2.dev, a competitor, claims roughly 50ms p99 same-region acknowledgment latency using stateful backends flushing multi-tenant objects, arguing the object-storage opportunity extends below 100ms via S3 Express and GCS rapid buckets.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Startups may compete on latency while keeping object-storage unit economics.

insights.claim: The core tension in object-storage streaming is how long to linger before flushing, trading latency directly against PUT API costs.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Unit economics of these services hinge on cloud object-storage request pricing.
insights.quote: you have to trade off directly between latency and cost of your API ops for PUTs
insights.locator: One of the tensions of course

insights.claim: Commenters compared K2 to AutoMQ and WarpStream and noted Kafka itself now supports diskless topics; one argued K2 makes sense mainly inside the Cloudflare ecosystem, not standalone.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: K2 is an ecosystem lock-in play more than a standalone Kafka displacer.
insights.locator: Several commenters asked how K2 differs

insights.claim: K2 charges $0.04/GB produced and the same to consume, plus $0.02/GB-month retention, so fan-out consumer patterns become expensive quickly; nothing is billed during beta.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Consume pricing may limit adoption for fan-out, a use case Cloudflare targets.
insights.quote: fan-out consumer strategies get very expensive very fast
insights.locator: Pricing drew the other substantive objection

insights.claim: A commenter argued K2's advantage over Google Pub/Sub is cost, especially for long retention, and that it is much cheaper than self-hosted Kafka, Amazon MSK or Confluent with no clusters to manage.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Price pressure on managed Kafka incumbents like Confluent.
insights.locator: The same commenter defended the cost case

insights.claim: K2's tech lead is 'not a huge fan' of the Kafka API, calling it too low level for users and too high level for deep integration; K2 uses a lease-based consume API suited to many low-powered Workers, though Kafka compatibility is on the roadmap.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals API divergence from Kafka standard, a risk/opportunity for Kafka ecosystem vendors.
insights.locator: Kafka compatibility is on the roadmap

insights.claim: Beta limits are 10GB storage and 30 MB/s produce per stream; key-based ordering, multi-GB/s writes, push-based Worker consumers, a lower-latency express tier and Kafka client support are future work.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Product is early; enterprise-grade features remain on roadmap.
